summary.text: The polynomial remainder theorem, also called little Bézout's theorem, says that dividing a polynomial f(x) by x − r leaves f(r) as the remainder.
As a result, x − r divides f(x) exactly when f(r) = 0, a property known as the factor theorem.
Because synthetic division is computationally easier, the function can be evaluated more cheaply by finding that remainder.

facts.label: Other name
facts.value: Little Bézout's theorem, after Étienne Bézout

facts.label: Worked example
facts.value: Dividing by x − 3 leaves remainder −123, so f(3) = −123

facts.label: Factor theorem
facts.value: x − r divides f(x) exactly when f(r) = 0

facts.label: Quotient degree
facts.value: The quotient has degree one less than f

facts.label: Factorizing
facts.value: Repeated use of the factor theorem can factorize a polynomial

items.prompt: You divide a polynomial f(x) by x − 4. Which quantity do you get as the remainder?

options.label: f(−4), the value at the opposite number
f(4), the value of the polynomial at 4
The leading coefficient of f
The constant term of f

items.explain: The remainder of the division of f(x) by x − r is f(r), here the value at 4.

items.prompt: You find that a polynomial's value at 3 is zero. What does this tell you about dividing it by x − 3?

options.label: The quotient must be zero as well
The remainder is 3, the input used
Nothing is left over, so x − 3 divides it
x − 3 cannot divide it without leftovers

items.explain: x − r is a divisor of f(x) if and only if f(r) = 0. The remainder is f(r), so a zero value means nothing is left over.

items.prompt: You want a polynomial's value at a point by way of the remainder. Of the two division methods, which is cheaper?

options.label: Synthetic division, which is computationally easier
Long division, which is more thorough
They cost the same, since both give the same remainder
Long division, which has fewer steps to copy

items.explain: Synthetic division is computationally easier, so the function can be evaluated more cheaply this way. Long division is described as more difficult.

items.prompt: A polynomial of degree 5 is divided by x − r. What degree does the quotient have?

options.label: Degree 5, the same as f
Degree 6, one more than f
Degree 3, two less than f
Degree 4, one less than f

items.explain: Any polynomial f(x) is f(r) plus the product of x − r and a polynomial of degree one less than f.

items.prompt: You want to break a polynomial into smaller factors. How does this theorem help?

options.label: Find an r where the value is zero, divide out x − r, and repeat on what remains
Evaluate at any r and use the result as a factor
Divide by x − r until the remainder reaches zero
Evaluate once and stop, since one value fixes all factors

items.explain: If the remainder is zero, the linear divisor is a factor. Repeated application of the factor theorem may be used to factorize the polynomial.

items.prompt: The remainder theorem is described as an application of which operation?

options.label: Completing the square
Euclidean division of polynomials
Graphing a function on axes
The quadratic formula

items.explain: The polynomial remainder theorem is an application of Euclidean division of polynomials.
